decks.title: System design fundamentals
decks.summary: The building blocks every design interview leans on.

cards.q: What do you do in the first five minutes of a system design interview?
cards.a: Clarify scope before drawing anything: core use cases, who the users are, scale (DAU, QPS, data size), latency and availability targets, and what is explicitly out of scope. Write the assumptions down; they drive every later trade-off.

cards.q: Horizontal vs. vertical scaling?
cards.a: Vertical: a bigger machine; simple, but has a ceiling and a single point of failure. Horizontal: more machines behind a load balancer; near-unbounded and fault tolerant, but needs stateless services or partitioned state.

cards.q: Why are stateless services easier to scale?
cards.a: Any instance can serve any request, so you add or remove instances freely and a crash loses nothing. Session and user state move to a shared store (cache or database), which becomes the thing you scale carefully.

cards.q: Layer 4 vs. layer 7 load balancing?
cards.a: L4 routes on IP and port; fast and protocol-agnostic. L7 reads the HTTP request, so it can route by path, header or cookie, terminate TLS, retry and do canaries, at the cost of more CPU per request.

cards.q: Cache-aside vs. write-through vs. write-back?
cards.a: Cache-aside: app reads the cache, falls back to the DB and fills the cache. Write-through: writes go to cache and DB together (consistent, slower writes). Write-back: writes hit the cache and flush later (fast, risks loss on crash).

cards.q: What causes a cache stampede and how do you prevent it?
cards.a: A hot key expires and thousands of requests miss at once and hammer the database. Fixes: request coalescing (single flight), a lock or lease on refill, serving stale while revalidating, and jittered TTLs.

cards.q: When do you reach for a CDN?
cards.a: For static or cacheable content read far more than written, and for users spread across regions. It cuts latency and origin load. Watch invalidation, cache-key design and cost for long-tail content.

cards.q: SQL or NoSQL: how do you choose?
cards.a: Start from access patterns. Relational fits rich queries, joins and transactions. Key-value, wide-column or document stores fit huge scale with simple, known access paths and flexible schemas. Many systems use both.

cards.q: What is database sharding and what does it cost?
cards.a: Splitting data across nodes by a shard key so writes and storage scale out. Costs: cross-shard queries and transactions get hard, hot shards appear with skewed keys, and resharding needs a migration plan.

cards.q: How do you pick a shard key?
cards.a: High cardinality, even distribution, and aligned with the dominant query so most requests hit one shard. Avoid monotonic keys (timestamps, auto-increment) that funnel writes to one shard.

cards.q: Why put a message queue between services?
cards.a: To decouple producers from consumers: it absorbs bursts, lets each side scale and fail independently, and enables retries and fan-out. You trade immediate consistency and simple debugging for resilience.

cards.q: What does back-of-the-envelope estimation buy you?
cards.a: A sanity check on the design's scale: QPS, peak QPS (2-3x average), storage per year and bandwidth. It tells you whether one database is enough, whether you need caching, and where the bottleneck will be.

cards.q: What are the latency numbers every engineer should know (roughly)?
cards.a: L1 cache ~1 ns, main memory ~100 ns, SSD random read ~100 µs, round trip in a datacenter ~0.5 ms, disk seek ~10 ms, cross-continent round trip ~150 ms. Memory is ~1000x faster than SSD, which is ~100x faster than disk.

cards.q: How do you design a good API for a system design question?
cards.a: Name resources and verbs clearly, make writes idempotent (idempotency keys), paginate with cursors, version the API, and return enough for the client to avoid extra round trips. State the core endpoints before the architecture.

cards.q: What is the difference between availability and durability?
cards.a: Availability: the system answers requests (e.g. 99.99% = ~52 min down a year). Durability: data, once acknowledged, is never lost (e.g. eleven nines in S3). A system can be durable but briefly unavailable.

cards.q: What does the CAP theorem actually say?
cards.a: When a network partition happens, a replicated system must choose between consistency (every read sees the latest write) and availability (every request gets an answer). Without a partition you can have both, so CAP is about behavior during failure.

cards.q: What does PACELC add to CAP?
cards.a: Else, even without a partition, you trade Latency against Consistency. Synchronous replication costs latency on every write; that trade-off is the one you pay day to day.

cards.q: Linearizability vs. serializability?
cards.a: Linearizability: single-object recency; once a write completes, all later reads see it. Serializability: multi-object transactions behave as if run one at a time, in some order. Strict serializability gives both.

cards.q: What is eventual consistency and what goes wrong with it?
cards.a: If writes stop, replicas converge. Meanwhile users can see stale data, lose their own writes on a different replica, or see time go backwards. Session guarantees (read-your-writes, monotonic reads) patch the worst cases.

cards.q: Explain quorums with N, R and W.
cards.a: Data lives on N replicas; a write waits for W acks, a read asks R replicas. If R + W > N, the read and write sets overlap, so a read sees the latest acknowledged write (absent sloppy quorums). Tune R and W for read or write speed.

cards.q: Leader-based, multi-leader and leaderless replication?
cards.a: Single leader: simple, consistent writes, leader is a bottleneck and failover point. Multi-leader: writes in several regions, needs conflict resolution. Leaderless (Dynamo): any replica takes writes, quorums plus read repair.

cards.q: How does Raft elect a leader?
cards.a: Followers that miss heartbeats for a randomized timeout become candidates, bump the term and request votes. A node votes once per term, only for a candidate whose log is at least as up to date. A majority wins; randomized timeouts avoid split votes.

cards.q: Why can't you order events across machines with wall clocks?
cards.a: Clocks drift and NTP corrections can jump them backwards, so two machines' timestamps can disagree by milliseconds or more. Use logical clocks (Lamport, vector), hybrid logical clocks, or bounded-uncertainty time like TrueTime.

cards.q: Lamport clocks vs. vector clocks?
cards.a: A Lamport clock gives a total order consistent with causality, but can't tell you whether two events were concurrent. A vector clock keeps one counter per node, so it can detect concurrency, at the cost of size growing with nodes.

cards.q: What is split brain and how do fencing tokens prevent damage?
cards.a: Two nodes both believe they are leader after a partition or GC pause. A fencing token is a monotonically increasing number from the lock service; storage rejects writes carrying an older token, so the stale leader can't corrupt data.

cards.q: Why is two-phase commit called blocking?
cards.a: If the coordinator crashes after participants vote yes, they must hold their locks until it returns; they can't decide alone. Consensus-replicated coordinators (e.g. Spanner) or sagas avoid that.

cards.q: What is the saga pattern?
cards.a: A long transaction split into local steps, each with a compensating action. On failure, run the compensations in reverse. You get availability and loose coupling but give up isolation, so design for intermediate states.

cards.q: At-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once delivery?
cards.a: At-most-once: may lose messages. At-least-once: retries, may duplicate. Exactly-once in practice means at-least-once delivery plus idempotent or transactional processing (dedup keys, transactional offsets).

cards.q: What is the transactional outbox pattern?
cards.a: Write the business change and an "event to publish" row in the same local transaction; a relay reads the outbox table (or CDC log) and publishes. It removes the dual-write problem between database and broker.

cards.q: What are CRDTs good for?
cards.a: Conflict-free replicated data types merge concurrent updates deterministically without coordination: counters, sets, registers, sequences. Good for offline-first apps, collaborative editing and multi-region active-active state.

cards.q: How do Merkle trees help anti-entropy?
cards.a: Replicas hash key ranges into a tree and compare roots; only differing subtrees are walked and exchanged. Synchronizing two large replicas costs bandwidth proportional to the differences, not the data size.

cards.q: What does the FLP result say?
cards.a: In a fully asynchronous system with even one crash-faulty process, no deterministic consensus protocol can guarantee termination. Real systems escape with timeouts (partial synchrony) or randomization.

decks.title: Reliability and operations
decks.summary: Keeping large systems up, and recovering fast.

cards.q: SLI, SLO, SLA?
cards.a: SLI: a measured indicator (e.g. % of requests under 300 ms). SLO: the internal target for it (99.9%). SLA: the contract with customers, with penalties, set looser than the SLO.

cards.q: What is an error budget used for?
cards.a: 1 − SLO is the unreliability you may spend. While budget remains, ship fast; when it's burned, freeze risky launches and invest in reliability. It turns reliability debates into data.

cards.q: How do retries cause outages, and how do you make them safe?
cards.a: Retries multiply load on an already struggling service (retry storms). Use exponential backoff with jitter, retry budgets or caps, idempotent operations, and only retry errors that are actually transient.

cards.q: What is a circuit breaker?
cards.a: A client-side switch that stops calling a failing dependency after an error threshold, fails fast for a cool-down, then lets a trial request through. It protects both the caller's resources and the struggling service.

cards.q: What is backpressure?
cards.a: A way for a slow consumer to signal producers to slow down (bounded queues, flow-control windows, rejecting work). Without it, queues grow until latency explodes or memory runs out.

cards.q: What is load shedding?
cards.a: Deliberately rejecting some requests (lowest priority first) when near capacity, so the requests you do accept still meet their SLO. Better a fast 503 for some than timeouts for everyone.

cards.q: What is a cascading failure?
cards.a: One component's failure overloads its neighbors, which fail and spread the load further, e.g. a cache outage sending all traffic to the database. Defenses: timeouts, circuit breakers, load shedding, bulkheads, capacity headroom.

cards.q: What are bulkheads?
cards.a: Isolating resources (thread pools, connection pools, cells, shards) per dependency or tenant so one bad actor can only sink its own compartment.

cards.q: What is cell-based architecture?
cards.a: Splitting a service into independent, identical cells, each serving a slice of customers with its own stack. Blast radius of a bad deploy or poison request is one cell; scaling means adding cells.

cards.q: Canary vs. blue-green deployment?
cards.a: Canary: send a small slice of traffic to the new version, compare metrics, then ramp. Blue-green: run the new version alongside, switch all traffic at once, keep the old one for instant rollback.

cards.q: Metrics, logs and traces: what is each for?
cards.a: Metrics: cheap aggregates for dashboards and alerts. Logs: detailed events for debugging one request. Traces: the path and timing of one request across services. Good observability links all three.

cards.q: Why alert on symptoms rather than causes?
cards.a: Users feel symptoms (errors, latency); causes (CPU high) are often harmless. Page on SLO burn rate; keep cause-based signals for dashboards and diagnosis to avoid alert fatigue.

cards.q: What makes a good postmortem?
cards.a: Blameless, timeline-based, focused on contributing factors and why defenses failed, with owned, prioritized action items. The goal is learning that changes the system, not a culprit.

decks.title: Databases and storage
decks.summary: How data is stored, indexed and kept correct.

cards.q: B-tree vs. LSM-tree?
cards.a: B-tree updates pages in place; fast reads, moderate write amplification. LSM-tree appends to a memtable and flushes sorted files merged by compaction; very fast writes, reads may check several files (helped by Bloom filters).

cards.q: What does a write-ahead log guarantee?
cards.a: Changes are appended to a durable log before data pages are modified, so after a crash the database replays the log to a consistent state. It also feeds replication and change data capture.

cards.q: What are the ACID isolation levels and their anomalies?
cards.a: Read uncommitted (dirty reads), read committed (non-repeatable reads), repeatable read / snapshot isolation (write skew), serializable (none). Most databases default to read committed or snapshot.

cards.q: What is write skew?
cards.a: Two transactions read the same data, each makes a decision, and each writes a different row, breaking an invariant (e.g. two doctors both go off call). Snapshot isolation allows it; fix with serializable isolation or locking the rows read.

cards.q: How does MVCC work?
cards.a: Each write creates a new row version tagged with a transaction id; readers see the snapshot valid at their start, so reads never block writes. Old versions are garbage-collected later (vacuum).

cards.q: What is an index and what does it cost?
cards.a: A separate structure (B-tree, hash, inverted) that finds rows without scanning. It speeds reads but slows every write and uses storage; index the columns your hot queries filter and sort on.

cards.q: When do you denormalize?
cards.a: When read paths need data from many tables and joins are too slow at scale. You trade storage and more complex writes (keeping copies in sync) for fast reads.

cards.q: What is change data capture?
cards.a: Streaming a database's committed changes from its log (e.g. Debezium on the binlog) to other systems: caches, search indexes, warehouses. It avoids dual writes and keeps derived data in order.

cards.q: How do you do a zero-downtime schema migration?
cards.a: Expand and contract: add the new column or table, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, then remove the old path. Every step stays backward compatible with the running code.

cards.q: Row store vs. column store?
cards.a: Row stores keep a record together; good for OLTP lookups and updates. Column stores keep each column together; compress well and scan only needed columns, good for analytics (OLAP).

cards.q: What is a Bloom filter?
cards.a: A compact bit array with k hash functions that answers "definitely not present" or "maybe present". No false negatives, tunable false positives. Used to skip disk reads in LSM trees and caches.

cards.q: How does consistent hashing reduce rebalancing?
cards.a: Nodes and keys hash onto a ring; each key goes to the next node clockwise. Adding or removing a node moves only about 1/N of keys. Virtual nodes smooth out the load.

decks.title: Design principles
decks.summary: The principles behind maintainable code and systems.

cards.q: State the Single Responsibility Principle.
cards.a: A module should have one reason to change, i.e. answer to one actor. It keeps changes local and code easier to test and understand.

cards.q: What is the Open/Closed Principle?
cards.a: Software should be open for extension but closed for modification: add behavior with new code (plugins, strategies, polymorphism) rather than editing stable, tested code.

cards.q: Explain the Liskov Substitution Principle.
cards.a: Subtypes must be usable wherever the base type is expected without surprising the caller: no stronger preconditions, no weaker postconditions. A square that breaks a rectangle's setters violates it.

cards.q: What is the Interface Segregation Principle?
cards.a: Clients shouldn't depend on methods they don't use. Prefer several small, role-specific interfaces over one fat one.

cards.q: What is the Dependency Inversion Principle?
cards.a: High-level policy shouldn't depend on low-level details; both depend on abstractions. It makes infrastructure swappable and logic testable with fakes.

cards.q: Coupling vs. cohesion?
cards.a: Cohesion: how closely the parts of one module belong together (want high). Coupling: how much modules depend on each other's internals (want low). Together they decide how far a change ripples.

cards.q: What is the principle of least knowledge (Law of Demeter)?
cards.a: A unit should talk only to its immediate collaborators, not reach through chains like a.getB().getC().do(). It limits coupling to internal structure.

cards.q: Composition over inheritance: why?
cards.a: Inheritance couples a child to its parent's implementation and fixes behavior at compile time. Composition assembles behavior from small parts that can be swapped at runtime and tested alone.

cards.q: What does YAGNI warn against?
cards.a: Building for speculative future needs. Each unneeded abstraction costs design, code and maintenance now and often guesses wrong. Build for today's requirements, keep code easy to change.

cards.q: What is Conway's Law and how do you use it?
cards.a: Systems mirror the communication structure of the organizations that build them. Use it deliberately (the inverse Conway maneuver): shape teams around the architecture you want.

cards.q: Why "make illegal states unrepresentable"?
cards.a: Encode invariants in types and data models so invalid combinations can't be constructed. Whole classes of bugs then become compile errors instead of runtime checks.

cards.q: What does "design for failure" mean in practice?
cards.a: Assume every dependency will be slow or down. Set timeouts, retries with backoff, fallbacks and graceful degradation, and test them (chaos experiments) instead of hoping.

cards.q: What is idempotency and why does it matter for APIs?
cards.a: An idempotent operation has the same effect whether applied once or many times. With retries and at-least-once delivery everywhere, idempotency keys on writes prevent double charges and duplicate records.

cards.q: What is the end-to-end argument?
cards.a: Correctness guarantees (integrity, exactly-once, security) belong at the endpoints, because lower layers can't fully provide them. Lower layers may add the same checks only as a performance optimization.

cards.q: Two-way door vs. one-way door decisions?
cards.a: Two-way doors are reversible: decide quickly, delegate. One-way doors are costly to undo (data models, public APIs, vendor lock-in): slow down, write it up, get review.

decks.title: Algorithms and data structures
decks.summary: The patterns behind most coding rounds.

cards.q: When does a hash map beat a balanced tree?
cards.a: For exact-key lookup, insert and delete in O(1) average. Use a tree (O(log n)) when you need ordering: range queries, min/max, sorted iteration, or predictable worst-case time.

cards.q: What is the two-pointer technique good for?
cards.a: Sorted arrays and linked lists: pair sums, removing duplicates, merging, palindromes, and cycle detection (fast and slow pointers). It turns many O(n²) scans into O(n).

cards.q: When do you use a sliding window?
cards.a: For contiguous subarrays or substrings that satisfy a condition (longest substring without repeats, max sum of size k). Grow the right edge, shrink the left while the window is invalid: O(n).

cards.q: BFS vs. DFS?
cards.a: BFS explores level by level with a queue; it finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs. DFS goes deep with recursion or a stack; good for connectivity, cycle detection, topological order and backtracking.

cards.q: When do you use Dijkstra's algorithm, and when not?
cards.a: Shortest paths from one source with non-negative edge weights, O((V+E) log V) with a heap. With negative edges use Bellman-Ford; for all pairs, Floyd-Warshall; with a good heuristic, A*.

cards.q: What is a topological sort for?
cards.a: Ordering nodes of a DAG so every edge goes forward: build systems, course prerequisites, task scheduling. Kahn's algorithm (in-degree queue) also detects cycles.

cards.q: How do you recognize a dynamic programming problem?
cards.a: Optimal substructure plus overlapping subproblems: the answer composes from answers to smaller versions that repeat. Define the state, the recurrence and base cases; memoize top-down or tabulate bottom-up.

cards.q: What does a heap give you?
cards.a: O(1) access to the min or max and O(log n) insert and pop. Classic uses: top-k, merging k sorted lists, scheduling, Dijkstra, and running medians with two heaps.

cards.q: When is a trie the right structure?
cards.a: For prefix queries over many strings: autocomplete, spell check, IP routing (longest prefix match). Lookups cost O(length of key), independent of how many keys are stored.

cards.q: What is union-find used for?
cards.a: Tracking connected components under merges in near-constant time (path compression plus union by rank): Kruskal's MST, network connectivity, grouping equivalent items.

cards.q: What is binary search on the answer?
cards.a: When feasibility is monotonic in a parameter (capacity, speed, time), binary search that parameter and test feasibility each step: O(log range × check).

cards.q: How do you find the top-k items in a stream?
cards.a: Keep a min-heap of size k: O(n log k). For heavy hitters in huge streams with bounded memory, use Count-Min Sketch plus a heap, or Misra-Gries.

cards.q: How does HyperLogLog estimate cardinality?
cards.a: It hashes items and tracks the maximum run of leading zeros per register; more distinct items produce longer runs. With ~12 KB it estimates billions of distinct values within ~1-2% error.

decks.title: Scalable system designs
decks.summary: One-line answers to the classic design prompts.

cards.q: URL shortener: how do you generate short codes?
cards.a: Base62-encode a unique 64-bit id (from a ticket server or Snowflake-style generator), or hash the URL and resolve collisions. Seven Base62 characters give ~3.5 trillion codes. Cache hot redirects; use 301 vs. 302 deliberately (302 if you need click analytics).

cards.q: Rate limiter: which algorithm and where?
cards.a: Token bucket for bursts with an average rate; sliding window counter for accuracy with little memory. Keep counters in Redis with atomic Lua scripts, enforce at the API gateway, return 429 with retry headers.

cards.q: Unique ID generator: how does Snowflake work?
cards.a: A 64-bit id = timestamp (41 bits) + datacenter and machine ids (10 bits) + per-millisecond sequence (12 bits). Ids are roughly time-sorted and generated locally without coordination; watch clock skew.

cards.q: News feed: fan-out on write or on read?
cards.a: Fan-out on write pushes posts into followers' cached feeds: fast reads, expensive for celebrities. Fan-out on read builds the feed at request time. Most use a hybrid: push for normal users, pull for celebrities.

cards.q: Chat system: how do messages reach online users?
cards.a: Clients hold persistent WebSocket connections to chat servers; a presence service maps users to servers; messages go through a queue to the recipient's server. Store history in a wide-column store keyed by channel and time-ordered message id.

cards.q: Search autocomplete: what is the core data structure?
cards.a: A trie of prefixes with the top-k suggestions cached at each node, rebuilt offline from query logs and served from memory or a cache. Shard by prefix; filter unsafe suggestions.

cards.q: Web crawler: what keeps it polite and efficient?
cards.a: A URL frontier with per-host queues and delays, robots.txt respect, DNS caching, content dedup by hash, URL dedup with a Bloom filter, and priority by page importance and freshness.

cards.q: Notification system: what are the key pieces?
cards.a: An API that validates and enqueues, per-channel queues and workers (push, SMS, email), third-party providers, user preferences and rate limits, retries with dedup, and delivery tracking.

cards.q: Video platform: how does upload and playback work?
cards.a: Upload to object storage via pre-signed URLs, transcode in a DAG of parallel jobs into many bitrates and formats, then serve through CDNs with adaptive bitrate streaming (HLS or DASH).

cards.q: Proximity service: how do you find nearby places fast?
cards.a: Index locations with geohash, quadtree or S2 cells; query the user's cell and its neighbors, then filter by distance. Business data is read-heavy and changes rarely, so replicate and cache it.

cards.q: Payment system: how do you avoid double charges?
cards.a: Idempotency keys on every payment request, a ledger with double-entry bookkeeping, exactly-once processing through idempotent consumers, and daily reconciliation against the payment provider.

cards.q: Distributed message queue: how does it scale?
cards.a: Topics split into partitions, each an append-only log replicated across brokers; consumers in a group split partitions; ordering holds within a partition; offsets let consumers replay.

cards.q: Real-time leaderboard: what data structure?
cards.a: A Redis sorted set: ZINCRBY to update a score, ZREVRANGE for the top N, ZREVRANK for a user's rank, all O(log n). Shard by score range or use approximate ranks at very large scale.

cards.q: Hotel reservation: how do you prevent overbooking?
cards.a: Keep per-room-type, per-date inventory rows and update them in a transaction with a check, using optimistic locking (version column) or a database constraint. Use idempotency keys for retries.

cards.q: What are the stages of an ML system in production?
cards.a: Data collection and labeling, feature pipelines, training, evaluation, deployment, monitoring for drift and quality, and a feedback loop that retrains. Most engineering effort sits in data and monitoring.

cards.q: What is training-serving skew?
cards.a: When features are computed differently at training and serving time, the model sees different inputs in production. Fix with a shared feature store or shared feature code and logging of served features.

cards.q: Online vs. batch inference?
cards.a: Batch precomputes predictions on a schedule; cheap, but stale. Online computes per request; fresh, but needs low-latency serving and autoscaling. Many systems mix both.

cards.q: What is retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)?
cards.a: Retrieve relevant documents (often by vector similarity) and add them to the model's prompt, so answers are grounded in current or private data without retraining. Quality depends mostly on chunking and retrieval.

cards.q: How does approximate nearest neighbor search work (e.g. HNSW)?
cards.a: HNSW builds a layered graph of vectors; search starts at the sparse top layer and greedily descends to dense layers. It trades a little recall for orders-of-magnitude speedups over brute force.

cards.q: How do you make LLM serving efficient?
cards.a: Continuous batching, KV-cache reuse (prefix caching), quantization, speculative decoding, tensor or pipeline parallelism across GPUs, and routing short requests away from long ones.

cards.q: How do you evaluate an LLM-powered feature?
cards.a: Build an eval set from real tasks, define pass criteria, score with exact checks, human review or LLM-as-judge (calibrated against humans), and track regressions on every prompt or model change.

cards.q: What is model or data drift?
cards.a: Data drift: the input distribution changes. Concept drift: the relationship between inputs and the right answer changes. Monitor input statistics and outcome metrics, and retrain or alert.

cards.q: Precision vs. recall?
cards.a: Precision: of what you flagged, how much was right. Recall: of what was really there, how much you caught. Choose by the cost of false positives vs. false negatives.

cards.q: What is an embedding?
cards.a: A dense vector representation where similar items sit close together, learned from data. Used for search, recommendations, clustering and as model inputs.

decks.title: Networking and the web
decks.summary: What happens between the client and your servers.

cards.q: What happens when you type a URL and hit enter?
cards.a: DNS resolves the name, the client opens a TCP (or QUIC) connection and a TLS handshake, sends the HTTP request through CDNs and load balancers to servers, gets the response, then parses, fetches subresources and renders.

cards.q: TCP vs. UDP?
cards.a: TCP: connection-oriented, reliable, ordered, congestion-controlled. UDP: connectionless datagrams with no guarantees; low overhead, used for DNS, real-time media and as the base for QUIC.

cards.q: What does HTTP/2 improve, and HTTP/3?
cards.a: HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams over one TCP connection with header compression, but TCP loss stalls all streams. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC (UDP) with per-stream loss recovery and faster handshakes.

cards.q: WebSockets vs. long polling vs. server-sent events?
cards.a: WebSockets: full-duplex persistent connection, for chat and games. SSE: one-way server push over HTTP, simple for feeds and progress. Long polling: fallback that holds requests open.

cards.q: What does TLS give you?
cards.a: Confidentiality (encryption), integrity (tamper detection) and server authentication via certificates. TLS 1.3 cuts the handshake to one round trip (zero with resumption).

cards.q: How does DNS-based load balancing work, and its limits?
cards.a: DNS returns different IPs by region, weight or health (GeoDNS). Limits: caching and TTLs delay failover, and the client's resolver location may not match the user's.

cards.q: REST vs. gRPC vs. GraphQL?
cards.a: REST: resource-oriented HTTP, universal and cacheable. gRPC: binary protobuf over HTTP/2, fast and typed, great between services. GraphQL: clients ask for exactly the fields they need, useful for varied front ends.

cards.q: What is anycast?
cards.a: Several servers announce the same IP address; routing sends each user to the nearest one. CDNs and DNS providers use it for low latency and DDoS absorption.

decks.title: Security
decks.summary: The questions that come up in every design review.

cards.q: Authentication vs. authorization?
cards.a: Authentication proves who you are (passwords, passkeys, tokens). Authorization decides what you may do (roles, policies, ACLs). Check authorization on every request at the server.

cards.q: How do OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect differ?
cards.a: OAuth 2.0 delegates access: an app gets a scoped access token to call an API on the user's behalf. OIDC adds identity on top: an ID token that says who the user is.

cards.q: Session cookies vs. JWTs?
cards.a: Server sessions are easy to revoke but need a shared store. JWTs are self-contained and stateless but hard to revoke before expiry. Use short-lived JWTs with refresh tokens, or sessions when revocation matters.

cards.q: How should passwords be stored?
cards.a: Never in plain text or with a fast hash. Use a slow, salted password hash (Argon2id, bcrypt or scrypt) with tuned cost, and prefer passkeys or MFA where you can.

cards.q: What is defense in depth?
cards.a: Layering independent controls (network rules, authentication, authorization, input validation, encryption, monitoring) so that one failure doesn't expose the system.

cards.q: What is the principle of least privilege?
cards.a: Give every user, service and credential only the permissions it needs, for only as long as it needs them. It limits the blast radius of a compromise.

cards.q: How do you protect secrets in a distributed system?
cards.a: Keep them in a secrets manager or KMS, never in code or images; inject at runtime, rotate regularly, scope per service, and audit access. Encrypt data with envelope encryption.

cards.q: What are the most common web vulnerabilities to design against?
cards.a: Injection (SQL, command), broken access control, XSS, CSRF, SSRF, insecure deserialization and misconfiguration. Use parameterized queries, output encoding, CSRF tokens, egress allowlists and secure defaults.

decks.title: Technical leadership
decks.summary: Behavioral questions for staff, principal and distinguished roles. Answers are frameworks, not scripts.

cards.q: How do you structure a behavioral answer?
cards.a: STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result, plus what you learned. Spend most of the time on your own actions and decisions, quantify the result, and pick stories at the scope of the level you are interviewing for.

cards.q: Tell me about a time you influenced without authority.
cards.a: Show how you built the case with data and prototypes, found the people whose problem it solved, wrote it down for broad review, adjusted to feedback, and made adopting it easy (paved path, migration help).

cards.q: Tell me about a technical decision you got wrong.
cards.a: Pick a real one with consequences. Explain your reasoning at the time, the signal that showed it was wrong, how quickly you reversed, what you did for the people affected, and the mechanism you changed so it doesn't recur.

cards.q: How do you handle a strong disagreement with another senior engineer?
cards.a: Separate the goal from the solution, agree on criteria first, compare options against them with data, time-box the debate, escalate cleanly if needed, then disagree and commit and support the decision fully.

cards.q: How do you decide what to work on as a principal engineer?
cards.a: Look for problems with the most leverage across teams: recurring incidents, scaling cliffs, slow developer workflows, strategic bets. Balance them against the business strategy and choose what only you are positioned to unblock.

cards.q: How do you write a good technical strategy?
cards.a: Diagnose the current state honestly, state guiding policies (the trade-offs you are choosing), and list coherent actions. Ground it in business goals, name what you're not doing, and revisit it as facts change.

cards.q: How do you grow other engineers?
cards.a: Delegate real problems with support, review designs with questions rather than answers, give specific feedback, sponsor people for visible work, and write down your reasoning so it scales beyond your meetings.

cards.q: How do you handle technical debt?
cards.a: Make it visible and quantified (incidents, velocity, cost), tie paydown to business outcomes, fix it incrementally alongside feature work, and stop adding new debt with guardrails and paved paths.

cards.q: How do you lead a large migration?
cards.a: Define the end state and success metrics, build tooling so teams migrate cheaply, go in waves starting with friendly teams, track progress publicly, handle the long tail with automation or ownership, and turn off the old system.

cards.q: Describe how you run an architecture review.
cards.a: Share a written design ahead of time, focus on requirements, risks and alternatives considered, probe failure modes and operability, record decisions and their rationale, and follow up on action items.

decks.title: Correctness and Data
decks.summary: Name the principle, then say what it claims.

cards.q: End-to-end argument: what does it say?
cards.a: A function that can only be completely and correctly implemented with knowledge held at the endpoints must be implemented at the endpoints; lower layers can only optimize it.

cards.q: Idempotency by default: what does it say?
cards.a: Every operation that can be retried should produce the same outcome whether it executes once or many times.

cards.q: One system of record per fact: what does it say?
cards.a: Each fact has exactly one authoritative owner; every other copy is a derived, explicitly stale view.

cards.q: Make illegal states unrepresentable: what does it say?
cards.a: Shape types, schemas and APIs so that invalid combinations cannot be constructed, rather than validating them after the fact.

cards.q: Expand–contract schema evolution: what does it say?
cards.a: Change shared schemas in backward-compatible steps: add the new form, migrate readers and writers, then remove the old form.

cards.q: Choose the consistency model explicitly: what does it say?
cards.a: Decide, per operation, what consistency the business requires, and make that choice visible rather than inheriting a store's default.

cards.q: No dual writes: what does it say?
cards.a: Never update two independent systems in sequence and hope both succeed; make one write authoritative and derive the other from it.

cards.q: Do not trust wall clocks for ordering: what does it say?
cards.a: Use logical ordering, versions or fencing tokens to sequence events and enforce exclusivity, not timestamps from independent machines.

decks.title: Failure and Resilience
decks.summary: Name the principle, then say what it claims.

cards.q: Static stability: what does it say?
cards.a: A system should keep doing what it was doing when a dependency fails, without needing to make any new decisions or acquire new resources.

cards.q: Blast radius and cells: what does it say?
cards.a: Partition the system into independent cells so that any single failure, bad deploy or poison request affects a bounded fraction of customers.

cards.q: Shuffle sharding: what does it say?
cards.a: Assign each customer a random combination of resources so that the failure caused by one customer rarely overlaps fully with another customer's resources.

cards.q: Constant work: what does it say?
cards.a: Design hot paths to do the same amount of work regardless of load or system state, so behavior under stress matches behavior in normal operation.

cards.q: Avoid bimodal behavior and risky fallback: what does it say?
cards.a: Avoid designs that have a rarely used operating mode; a fallback that is not exercised constantly will fail when you need it.

cards.q: Timeouts, retries, backoff and jitter, with budgets: what does it say?
cards.a: Every remote call needs a deliberate timeout, a bounded retry policy with exponential backoff and jitter, and a system-wide limit on retry amplification.

cards.q: Load shedding and graceful degradation: what does it say?
cards.a: When demand exceeds capacity, reject excess work early and cheaply, and degrade nonessential features before essential ones.

cards.q: Isolate dependencies with bulkheads: what does it say?
cards.a: Give each dependency its own bounded pool of resources so that one slow or failing dependency cannot exhaust capacity needed by others.

cards.q: Separate control plane from data plane: what does it say?
cards.a: Keep the components that configure the system apart from the components that serve traffic, so that the data plane keeps working when the control plane does not.

decks.title: Scale and Performance
decks.summary: Name the principle, then say what it claims.

cards.q: Bound everything and apply backpressure: what does it say?
cards.a: Every queue, buffer, pool, cache, batch and retry loop needs an explicit limit, and producers must slow down when consumers fall behind.

cards.q: Little's Law: what does it say?
cards.a: In a stable system, the average number of items in it equals the arrival rate times the average time each spends in it: L = λW.

cards.q: Amdahl's Law: what does it say?
cards.a: The speedup from improving part of a system is limited by the fraction of time spent in the part you did not improve.

cards.q: Measure the tail, not the average: what does it say?
cards.a: Design and set targets on high percentiles and their behavior under fan-out, because averages hide the experience of the users who matter most.

cards.q: Coordination is the scalability tax: what does it say?
cards.a: Scale comes from avoiding coordination; partition data and work along the access pattern so most operations touch one partition.

cards.q: Data gravity: what does it say?
cards.a: Data attracts computation and services toward itself, so place compute near data and treat moving large datasets as a costly, slow architectural event.

cards.q: Cost as an architectural attribute: what does it say?
cards.a: Treat cost per unit of business value as a first-class quality attribute, designed and reviewed like latency or availability.

decks.title: Simplicity and Evolvability
decks.summary: Name the principle, then say what it claims.

cards.q: Information hiding (Parnas): what does it say?
cards.a: Decompose systems into modules that each hide a design decision likely to change, exposing only an interface that does not reveal it.

cards.q: Mechanism vs policy: what does it say?
cards.a: Separate the mechanism that makes something possible from the policy that decides what to do, so policy can change without rewriting mechanism.

cards.q: Gall's Law: what does it say?
cards.a: A complex system that works is invariably found to have evolved from a simple system that worked; one designed from scratch never works and cannot be patched to work.

cards.q: Hyrum's Law: what does it say?
cards.a: With enough users of an API, every observable behavior will be depended on by somebody, regardless of what the contract promises.

cards.q: Postel's Law and its critique: what does it say?
cards.a: "Be conservative in what you send, liberal in what you accept" aids interoperability early, but at scale tolerance of malformed input becomes de facto protocol and a security risk.

cards.q: Choose boring technology: what does it say?
cards.a: Spend a limited budget of novelty only where it creates differentiated value; use proven, well-understood technology everywhere else.

cards.q: Prefer duplication over the wrong abstraction: what does it say?
cards.a: Tolerate duplication until the common pattern is clear; a premature shared abstraction is costlier than the duplication it removes.

cards.q: Design interfaces for evolution: what does it say?
cards.a: Treat every published interface as a long-lived product with explicit versioning, compatibility rules and a deprecation path.

decks.title: Operations and Change
decks.summary: Name the principle, then say what it claims.

cards.q: Immutable infrastructure: what does it say?
cards.a: Never modify running infrastructure in place; replace it with a new, versioned artifact built from source.

cards.q: Observability as a design input: what does it say?
cards.a: Decide what questions you will need to answer about the system in production before you build it, and design telemetry, identifiers and boundaries to answer them.

cards.q: Small, progressive, reversible changes: what does it say?
cards.a: Ship changes in small increments, expose them progressively to production, and make each one quickly reversible.

cards.q: Decouple deploy from release: what does it say?
cards.a: Separate putting code into production from exposing behavior to users, so each can be controlled, staged and reversed on its own.

cards.q: SLOs and error budgets: what does it say?
cards.a: Define reliability targets from the user's perspective, and use the remaining error budget to make explicit trade-offs between velocity and reliability.

cards.q: Chesterton's fence: what does it say?
cards.a: Do not remove or change an existing constraint until you understand why it was put there.

decks.title: Security
decks.summary: Name the principle, then say what it claims.

cards.q: Least privilege: what does it say?
cards.a: Every principal (person, service, workload, credential) should hold only the permissions it needs, for only as long as it needs them.

cards.q: Defense in depth: what does it say?
cards.a: Layer independent controls so that the failure or bypass of any single control does not lead to compromise.

cards.q: Fail closed vs fail open: what does it say?
cards.a: Decide explicitly, per control, whether failure should deny access (closed) or allow it (open), weighing security harm against availability harm.

cards.q: Secure by default and paved roads: what does it say?
cards.a: Make the secure path the easiest path, so teams get security as a property of the platform rather than as a checklist.

cards.q: Explicit trust boundaries: what does it say?
cards.a: Identify every point where data or control crosses between trust levels, and authenticate, authorize and validate at each one; no network location confers trust.

cards.q: Minimize attack surface and data held: what does it say?
cards.a: Expose the fewest interfaces and keep the least sensitive data possible; what you do not run or store cannot be attacked or leaked.

decks.title: Organizations and Decisions
decks.summary: Name the principle, then say what it claims.

cards.q: Conway's Law: what does it say?
cards.a: Organizations design systems whose structure mirrors their communication structure.

cards.q: Cognitive load as a constraint: what does it say?
cards.a: Size team responsibilities and system boundaries so that the people who own a system can hold it in their heads.

cards.q: Reversible vs irreversible decisions: what does it say?
cards.a: Make two-way-door decisions quickly and locally; slow down and widen review only for one-way doors that are costly or impossible to undo.

cards.q: Write decisions down with their context: what does it say?
cards.a: Record significant architectural decisions with the context, options considered and trade-offs accepted, so future readers can evaluate them rather than guess.

cards.q: You build it, you run it: what does it say?
cards.a: The team that builds a system should operate it in production, so the feedback from operating it shapes how it is built.

cards.q: Optimize the whole, not the parts: what does it say?
cards.a: Evaluate architectural choices by their effect on end-to-end outcomes, not on the metrics of the component or team that proposes them.

cards.q: Name the failure model: why?
cards.a: Every design should state what it tolerates: how many node crashes, which partitions, how much clock skew, whether disks can lie about fsync. Undocumented assumptions become production incidents.

cards.q: Safety unconditional, liveness conditional: why?
cards.a: Prefer designs that may stall under bad conditions but never corrupt or lose committed data. Make stalls observable and recoverable.

cards.q: Buy the weakest consistency that is correct, and document it: why?
cards.a: Strong consistency where a stale read causes a wrong decision (money, uniqueness, permissions, leadership); session guarantees or eventual consistency elsewhere. Write down which is which per API.

cards.q: Never use wall-clock time for correctness without a bound: why?
cards.a: Use monotonic clocks for durations, logical or hybrid clocks for ordering, fencing tokens for exclusion, and an enforced maximum skew wherever time remains in the critical path.

cards.q: Every write path is idempotent: why?
cards.a: Assume every message will be delivered at least twice and every request retried. Design keys, conditional writes, and dedup records accordingly.

cards.q: Bound everything: why?
cards.a: Queues, retries, timeouts, concurrency, batch sizes, cache sizes, fan-out, and payloads. An unbounded resource is a future outage with an unknown trigger.

cards.q: Fail fast and shed early: why?
cards.a: A quick rejection is cheaper for everyone than a slow failure. Reject at the edge, before expensive work.

cards.q: Retry at one layer, with jitter and a budget: why?
cards.a: Multiplicative retries turn partial outages into total ones.

cards.q: Make the common transaction single-partition: why?
cards.a: Choose partition keys that align with the dominant access and transaction boundary. Cross-partition coordination should be the exception.

cards.q: Count failure domains, not replicas: why?
cards.a: Replicas that share power, network, software version, configuration, or deployment wave are one replica for correlated failures.

cards.q: Detect from the client's point of view: why?
cards.a: Health checks that exercise trivial paths miss gray failures. Measure what users experience and alert on it.

cards.q: Fence the past: why?
cards.a: Every leader, lease, and configuration has an epoch. Stale actors must be rejected by the resource they touch, not trusted to know they are stale.

cards.q: Keep consensus small: why?
cards.a: Put metadata, leases, and configuration in a consensus system; keep bulk data and hot paths out of it.

cards.q: Design the recovery path, not just the steady state: why?
cards.a: Cold caches, rebuilds, rebalances, and restarts are when systems are most fragile. Rate-limit them and test them.

cards.q: Prefer static stability: why?
cards.a: During a dependency failure, a system should keep doing what it was doing (serve last known config, keep existing capacity) rather than needing the failed dependency to recover.

cards.q: Name the guarantee, then find the mechanism: why?
cards.a: For every invariant the business cares about (no double spend, no oversell, unique usernames), write down which mechanism enforces it: a constraint, a lock, serializable isolation or a single-writer design. "The database handles it" is not an answer.

cards.q: Push invariants into the database: why?
cards.a: Unique constraints, foreign keys, check and exclusion constraints, and conditional atomic updates are enforced correctly regardless of isolation level or application bugs. Application-level checks done with read-then-write are race conditions waiting for traffic.

cards.q: Default to the strongest isolation you can afford, and measure: why?
cards.a: Starting from serializable and relaxing per transaction with a written justification is safer than starting from Read Committed and discovering write skew in a financial audit.

cards.q: Retries are part of the transaction contract: why?
cards.a: Under serializable or optimistic concurrency, aborts are normal operation. Every transactional code path needs a bounded, idempotent retry wrapper, written once and shared across teams.

cards.q: Choose the storage engine for the steady-state workload, not the benchmark: why?
cards.a: Run long enough for compaction, vacuum and checkpoints to reach equilibrium, with realistic key distributions and dataset sizes several times larger than RAM.

cards.q: Durability is end-to-end: why?
cards.a: Count acknowledged-write loss scenarios across every layer: fsync settings, replication mode, disk caches, backup cadence and failover behavior. Write the answer down as an explicit RPO, and test it.

cards.q: Delay sharding, then shard deliberately: why?
cards.a: Scale up, add replicas, partition tables and split services first. When you do shard, choose the key from the dominant access pattern and transaction boundaries, and build resharding tooling before you need it.

cards.q: Design for skew: why?
cards.a: Assume Zipfian access patterns, giant tenants and celebrity keys. Every partitioning scheme needs a story for the 1% of keys that get 50% of the traffic.

cards.q: Failover must fence: why?
cards.a: Promotion without guaranteed demotion of the old leader is split brain waiting to happen. Prefer consensus-based leadership, or leases with fencing tokens, over heuristics.

cards.q: Make replication lag a first-class signal: why?
cards.a: Expose it, alert on it, and give applications read-your-writes primitives (LSN or GTID waits, leader pinning) instead of hoping lag stays small.

cards.q: Garbage collection is a production service: why?
cards.a: Vacuum, purge, compaction and tombstone cleanup need monitoring, capacity planning and owners. Long-running transactions are a resource leak and should be time-limited by policy.

cards.q: Plan stability beats plan optimality: why?
cards.a: For critical queries, a predictable plan that is good enough is worth more than one that is sometimes optimal and occasionally catastrophic. Pin, hint or track plans in the places that matter.

cards.q: Backups don't exist until restores are tested: why?
cards.a: Automate restore drills, measure restore time against your RTO, and verify the restored data, not just that the restore job exited zero.

cards.q: Prefer boring, well-understood databases: why?
cards.a: Every new engine adds failure modes your on-call engineers have never seen. The bar for introducing one should be a workload that the existing fleet demonstrably cannot serve.

cards.q: Round trips are the currency: why?
cards.a: For anything far from the user, latency is dominated by RTT count, not bandwidth or server time. Count handshakes, redirects, DNS lookups, and sequential fetches in every critical user path, and design to remove them.

cards.q: Reuse connections, but bound their lifetime: why?
cards.a: Pooling avoids handshakes and slow start. Unbounded lifetimes break load balancing, pin traffic to stale backends, and outlive middlebox state. Set a maximum connection age with jitter, and an idle timeout shorter than any NAT or firewall on the path.

cards.q: Timeouts nest, and every call has one: why?
cards.a: No network call without a deadline. Each layer's timeout is shorter than its caller's. Propagate deadlines (gRPC does this natively) so downstream work stops when the user has gone.

cards.q: Retry at one layer, with a budget: why?
cards.a: Choose one layer to own retries for each call path. Cap retries per request and as a fraction of total traffic (around 10% is a common budget). Retry only idempotent operations, with exponential backoff and jitter.

cards.q: Health is what the client experiences: why?
cards.a: Liveness probes check that a process exists. Readiness must reflect the ability to serve real traffic. Combine active checks with passive outlier detection, and set panic thresholds so a broken checker can't concentrate load.

cards.q: Balance the unit of work you care about: why?
cards.a: If requests vary in cost or ride multiplexed connections, balance requests at L7 or in the client, not connections at L4. Use P2C or least-request over round robin.

cards.q: Design for partial failure, not binary failure: why?
cards.a: Assume gray failure. Detect slow as well as dead. Prefer mechanisms that degrade (shed load, serve stale) over ones that cliff.

cards.q: Cache is an availability layer, not just a speed layer: why?
cards.a: stale-if-error, request collapsing, and origin shields let you survive origin outages. Treat cache-key and TTL changes as production changes with load implications.

cards.q: Know who caches your DNS: why?
cards.a: TTLs are advisory. Any failover based on DNS must assume a long tail of clients on old answers. Use anycast or LB-level failover when you need seconds, not minutes.

cards.q: Control planes fail static: why?
cards.a: Proxies, sidecars, and edges must keep serving with last-known-good config when the control plane is unreachable. A control-plane outage should freeze changes, not stop traffic.

cards.q: Stage config like code: why?
cards.a: Network config (routes, mesh policy, WAF rules, CDN rules, BGP) has a blast radius equal to its reach. Canary it per cell or region with automated rollback, exactly like a binary.

cards.q: Make the client's address and identity explicit: why?
cards.a: Carry original client IP and workload identity through every hop, trust those signals only from your own infrastructure, and authenticate service-to-service traffic with mTLS.

cards.q: Instrument the transport: why?
cards.a: Export retransmits, RTT, connection counts, pool saturation, DNS latency, and TLS handshake errors as first-class metrics. You can't debug what you only see in a pcap.

cards.q: Separate control plane from data plane: why?
cards.a: Keep the data plane simple, statically stable, and able to run on cached configuration. Accept a lower availability target for the control plane, and never put it in the request path.

cards.q: Design for static stability: why?
cards.a: Pre-provision enough capacity to survive the loss of an AZ (N+1 across zones) without launching anything. Recovery that requires the control plane at the moment of crisis is a recovery that may not happen.

cards.q: Bound blast radius explicitly: why?
cards.a: Use cells, shuffle sharding, per-tenant quotas, and progressive rollouts. Every change and every tenant should have a known maximum impact, and you should be able to state it as a number.

cards.q: Prefer level-triggered reconciliation: why?
cards.a: Controllers that compare desired state to observed state and converge are robust to missed events, restarts, and duplicates. Edge-triggered workflows that assume every event arrives exactly once are fragile.

cards.q: Requests are a contract; limits are a weapon: why?
cards.a: Set memory requests to real working-set usage and memory limits equal to requests. Be deliberate about CPU limits. They protect neighbors, but CFS throttling damages tail latency.

cards.q: Make shared limits visible: why?
cards.a: Track conntrack tables, ENI/IP quotas, etcd size, API server inflight requests, NAT ports, file descriptors, and per-account API rate limits. Hidden shared limits cause the outages nobody predicted.

cards.q: Keep failure domains aligned: why?
cards.a: Spread replicas, volumes, load balancer targets, and dependencies over the same zones. A service that is multi-AZ but whose database is single-AZ is single-AZ.

cards.q: Treat cross-zone and cross-region bytes as a design cost: why?
cards.a: Data transfer pricing and latency both reward locality. Make topology an explicit input to routing and placement.

cards.q: Choose isolation to match trust: why?
cards.a: Shared-kernel containers for trusted code. gVisor or microVMs for untrusted or multi-tenant code. Hardware or account boundaries for hard tenancy and compliance.

cards.q: The data tier determines your RPO and RTO: why?
cards.a: Design multi-region from the data model outward: who owns each record, how it replicates, and how you fence. Stateless failover is the easy part.

cards.q: Exercise every recovery path: why?
cards.a: A failover, restore, or region evacuation that hasn't been run recently should be assumed broken. Game days and continuous chaos testing turn hope into evidence.

cards.q: Avoid synchronized behavior: why?
cards.a: Add jitter to retries, cache expiries, cron schedules, and reconnects. Synchronized clients turn small blips into thundering herds against control planes.

cards.q: Paxos (single-decree and Multi-Paxos): what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Getting a set of unreliable, asynchronous processes to agree on one value, and then on a sequence of values, without ever disagreeing.

cards.q: Raft: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Replicated-log consensus designed to be understandable, with a strong leader and a log that only flows from leader to followers.

cards.q: Leader leases and fencing tokens: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Ensuring that a node that believes it holds a lock or leadership cannot corrupt shared state after it has silently lost that role.

cards.q: Two-phase commit: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Making a transaction that spans several independent resource managers commit everywhere or nowhere.

cards.q: Percolator-style transactions: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Snapshot-isolated, multi-row ACID transactions layered on a sharded key-value store that only offers single-row atomicity.

cards.q: Viewstamped Replication and ZAB (compared with Raft): what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Two leader-based replicated-log protocols, older than Raft and closely related to it, that differ mainly in how a new leader obtains the log.

cards.q: Lamport clocks: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Giving events in a distributed system timestamps that respect causality, without synchronized physical clocks.

cards.q: Vector clocks: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Capturing the full causal order between events so that concurrent updates can be detected rather than silently ordered.

cards.q: Hybrid Logical Clocks: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Timestamps that respect causality like Lamport clocks yet stay within a bounded distance of physical time, using commodity NTP.

cards.q: TrueTime and commit-wait: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Achieving external consistency (linearizable transactions globally) by making clock uncertainty explicit and waiting it out.

cards.q: Gossip (epidemic dissemination): what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Spreading information to every node of a large, churning cluster with no central coordinator, at low per-node cost.

cards.q: SWIM: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Scalable membership and failure detection with constant per-node load and a false-positive rate that does not grow with cluster size.

cards.q: Phi accrual failure detector: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Replacing a binary "alive/dead" timeout with a continuous suspicion level that adapts to observed network behavior.

cards.q: Chandy-Lamport snapshots: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Recording a consistent global state of a running distributed system, including in-flight messages, without stopping it.

cards.q: Quorum reads/writes (W+R>N) with read repair and hinted handoff: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Tunable consistency and availability for leaderless replicated storage by requiring overlapping sets of replicas for reads and writes.

cards.q: Merkle-tree anti-entropy: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Finding and fixing the differences between two large replicas while exchanging data proportional to the difference, not the dataset.

cards.q: CRDTs (G-Counter, PN-Counter, OR-Set, LWW-Register): what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Data types whose replicas can be updated independently and always converge to the same value when they exchange state, with no coordination.

cards.q: Chain replication: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Strongly consistent, high-throughput primary-backup replication by arranging replicas in a line instead of a star.

cards.q: B+-tree: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Keeps a large sorted key space on block storage so that point lookups, range scans and updates each touch only a handful of pages.

cards.q: LSM-tree compaction (leveled vs tiered): what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Turns random writes into sequential ones by buffering in memory and merging sorted immutable files in the background, then trades write, read and space amplification through the compaction policy.

cards.q: MVCC visibility and Serializable Snapshot Isolation: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Lets readers and writers proceed without blocking each other by keeping multiple row versions, and adds a cheap runtime check so that snapshot reads still give serializable results.

cards.q: ARIES write-ahead-log recovery: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Restores a database to a consistent state after a crash while letting the buffer manager write dirty pages whenever it likes (steal) and not forcing them at commit (no-force).

cards.q: Reed-Solomon erasure coding: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Tolerates the loss of any m out of k+m storage fragments at far less overhead than replication.

cards.q: Bloom filter: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Answers "is x possibly in the set?" in a few bits per element, with no false negatives and a tunable false-positive rate.

cards.q: Cuckoo filter: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: An approximate set-membership structure like a Bloom filter that also supports deletion, and is smaller at low false-positive rates.

cards.q: HyperLogLog: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Estimates the number of distinct elements in a huge stream using kilobytes of memory and a few percent or less error, with lossless merging.

cards.q: Count-Min sketch: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Estimates per-key frequencies in a high-volume stream in sublinear space, with a one-sided, bounded overestimate.

cards.q: t-digest: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Estimates quantiles such as p50, p99 and p99.9 from streaming or distributed data in small, mergeable space, with the best accuracy at the tails.

cards.q: Reservoir sampling: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Maintains a uniform random sample of k items from a stream of unknown, possibly unbounded length in O(k) memory.

cards.q: MinHash and LSH: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Estimates Jaccard similarity between large sets cheaply, and finds near-duplicate pairs among millions of items without comparing every pair.

cards.q: Consistent hashing with virtual nodes: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Maps keys to a changing set of nodes so that adding or removing a node moves only about 1/N of the keys, while keeping load balanced.

cards.q: Rendezvous (HRW) hashing: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Lets every client pick the same owner (or top-r owners) for a key from a node list, with minimal disruption, no ring and no shared state beyond the list.

cards.q: Jump consistent hash: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Maps a key to one of n numbered buckets with perfect balance, zero memory and minimal movement when n grows.

cards.q: Maglev hashing: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Gives a software load balancer an O(1) per-packet backend lookup with near-perfect balance and minimal disruption when backends change.

cards.q: Skip list: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Provides an ordered in-memory map with expected O(log n) search, insert and delete, simple to implement and easy to make concurrent or lock-free.

cards.q: Token bucket, leaky bucket and GCRA: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Enforce a long-run rate while allowing a bounded burst, cheaply and per key.

cards.q: Exponential backoff with jitter and retry budgets: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Recover from transient failure without turning a blip into a self-sustaining retry storm.

cards.q: Circuit breaker state machine: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Stop sending calls to a dependency that is failing, so callers fail fast and the dependency can recover.

cards.q: Adaptive concurrency limits (AIMD, Vegas/Gradient style): what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Find and enforce the number of in-flight requests a service can handle without a hand-tuned constant.

cards.q: CoDel queue management: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Keep queues from turning into standing delay (bufferbloat) while still absorbing short bursts.

cards.q: Hedged requests: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Cut tail latency by sending a duplicate request when the first is slower than usual.

cards.q: Power of two choices (with peak-EWMA): what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Spread load nearly as well as global least-loaded, without global state or herding.

cards.q: TCP CUBIC: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Fill high bandwidth-delay-product paths quickly while remaining fair to other loss-based flows.

cards.q: BBR congestion control: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Run at the bottleneck's bandwidth with minimal queue, using a model of the path rather than loss as the signal.

cards.q: LRU, LFU, ARC and W-TinyLFU: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Decide which items to keep in a fixed-size cache so the hit rate stays high across changing access patterns.

cards.q: Little's Law and the M/M/1 queue: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Relate concurrency, throughput and latency, and predict how latency explodes as utilization rises.

cards.q: Universal Scalability Law: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Model how throughput scales with concurrency or nodes, including the point where adding more makes it worse.

cards.q: Transformer attention and the KV cache: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Let every token draw on every earlier token, and avoid recomputing that history at each decoding step.

cards.q: Continuous batching and PagedAttention: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Keep GPUs busy serving many variable-length generations without wasting KV-cache memory.

cards.q: Speculative decoding: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Generate several tokens per expensive forward pass of a large model, without changing its output distribution.

cards.q: Quantization (INT8/INT4, GPTQ/AWQ-style): what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Shrink model weights (and sometimes activations and KV cache) to fewer bits to cut memory and bandwidth with minimal quality loss.

cards.q: HNSW vector search: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Find approximate nearest neighbours in high-dimensional embeddings with high recall and low latency.

cards.q: IVF-PQ vector search: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Search billions of vectors in limited memory by clustering the space and compressing each vector to a few bytes.

cards.q: BM25 and hybrid retrieval with Reciprocal Rank Fusion: what problem does it solve?
cards.a: Retrieve documents that match exact terms and meaning, then merge lexical and vector rankings robustly.
